```{python}
V.animate(p3_frame, 8, captions=p3_caps, interval=1300)
```

Frames 1–4 fold a set over positions; frames 5–8 sieve the value domain from the divisor side.

:::

**Reading the animation.** Frames 1–4 are A2's chain rule applied to *subsequences* instead of subarrays: each row keeps only the distinct gcds reachable so far, and the rows never get long — three is the ceiling for values under $16$, matching $\lceil \log_2 10 \rceil + 1$. Frames 5–8 abandon positions entirely: the divisor table $c[d]$ is built once in $\sum_d V / d$ reads, $\binom{c_d}{2}$ is the *at-least* count, and the top-down subtraction is what makes it an *exact* count — the cyan and green cells are the two $d$ values that survive the inversion, and flattening them gives the same sorted list a brute-force pair loop would produce, at a fraction of the cost. @sec-gcd-p3-subseq is the reachability question, @sec-gcd-p3-gcdpair the counting one.

{{< include ../problems/lc-1819-number-of-different-subsequences-gcds/problem.qmd >}}

[**From "does it exist" to "how many land here."** 1819 asks which gcd values are reachable at all, and answers with a set. 3312 asks how many *pairs* reach each value, and answers with a histogram — the same divisor loop, but $c[d]$ now feeds $\binom{c_d}{2}$ instead of a gcd test.]{.flow-bridge}

{{< include ../problems/lc-3312-sorted-gcd-pair-queries/problem.qmd >}}

## Pattern 4: Run a Residue Histogram Under Moves {#sec-gcd-p4}

**From values to residues.** Pattern 3 kept the whole value domain in view. Pattern 4 throws almost all of it away: when every operation in the statement only ever touches $a_i \bmod k$, the array *is* a $k$-cell histogram and nothing else (A3). The first problem here spends moves to *equalise* the three buckets of a $3$-cycle; the second spends a rising counter to *serve* the buckets on a schedule. Neither one needs to know which element is in which bucket, only how many are — and once the question is posed on the histogram, the answer is arithmetic on counters, not a search.

::: {.callout-important title="Template"}
- **Bucket by residue, not value.** `cnt[r] = #{i : a[i] % k == r}`; every later decision reads `cnt`, never $a$ itself (@sec-gcd-a3).
- **A move is a transfer between buckets.** Adding $1$ to an element walks it from bucket $r$ to bucket $(r + 1) \bmod k$ — so the operation becomes bookkeeping between two counters, not a mutation of the array.
- **Only forward moves means one pass.** When surplus can only be pushed in one direction around the cycle, a single sweep handing each bucket's excess to its successor is optimal — no backtracking, no choosing which element to move.
- **A schedule over buckets is a max, not a sum.** When operations must happen at distinct times $x = 1, 2, 3, \ldots$ and each $x$ can serve one element, the cost is the *last* $x$ spent: $(\mathit{count}[d] - 1) \cdot k + d$ for the busiest need $d$ (@sec-gcd-a3).
:::

::: {#fig-gcd-anim-p4}

```{python}
#| echo: false
p4_arr = Traces.BR_ARR                      # [0, 2, 5, 5, 4, 8]
p4_target = len(p4_arr) // 3
p4_cnt = [sum(1 for x in p4_arr if x % 3 == r) for r in range(3)]
p4_rows, p4_moves = [list(p4_cnt)], 0
for _ in range(3):
    for p4_r in range(3):
        if p4_cnt[p4_r] > p4_target:
            p4_extra = p4_cnt[p4_r] - p4_target
            p4_cnt[p4_r] -= p4_extra
            p4_cnt[(p4_r + 1) % 3] += p4_extra
            p4_moves += p4_extra
            p4_rows.append(list(p4_cnt))
assert p4_rows[0] == [1, 1, 4] and p4_target == 2
assert p4_rows == [[1, 1, 4], [3, 1, 2], [2, 2, 2]], p4_rows
assert p4_moves == Traces.BR_ANS == 3
p4_zr_arr, p4_k = Traces.ZR_ARR, Traces.ZR_K        # [1, 2, 1, 3], k = 3
p4_need = Counter()
for p4_x in p4_zr_arr:
    p4_r = p4_x % p4_k
    if p4_r:
        p4_need[p4_k - p4_r] += 1
p4_raw = max((p4_cnt2 - 1) * p4_k + p4_d for p4_d, p4_cnt2 in p4_need.items())
p4_zans = p4_raw + 1
assert dict(p4_need) == {2: 2, 1: 1} and p4_raw == 5
assert p4_zans == Traces.ZR_ANS == 6
p4_caps = [
    "a = [0, 2, 5, 5, 4, 8]: count residues mod 3 -> buckets [1, 1, 4]",
    "target is n/3 = 2 per bucket; bucket 2 has 2 surplus -> push both forward",
    "buckets are now [3, 1, 2]; bucket 0 has 1 surplus -> push it forward",
    "buckets [2, 2, 2], settled; total moves 2 + 1 = 3, the answer",
    "switch: a = [1, 2, 1, 3], k = 3 - a schedule, not a balance",
    "remainder 1 (two elements) needs x = 2 mod 3; remainder 2 (one) needs x = 1",
    "need = {x=2: 2, x=1: 1}; the busiest need decides the last x spent",
    f"moves = max_d (count[d]-1)*k + d + 1 = {p4_raw} + 1 = {p4_zans}",
]


def p4_frame(ax, p, t):
    if t <= 3:
        V.grid(ax, p, [["bucket r", "r=0", "r=1", "r=2"],
                       ["count", *[str(x) for x in p4_rows[min(t, len(p4_rows) - 1)]]]],
               colors={(1, min(t + 1, 3) if t <= 1 else 3): "amber"} if t <= 1 else
                      {(1, 3): "green"}, cell_w=1.1)
        V.text(ax, p, 0, -0.9, f"moves so far = {0 if t == 0 else (2 if t == 1 else (3 if t == 2 else 3))}",
               size=9, color="muted", ha="left")
    else:
        V.grid(ax, p, [["element", "1", "2", "1", "3"],
                       ["x mod 3", "1", "2", "1", "0"],
                       ["needs x", "2", "1", "2", "-"]],
               colors={(2, 1): "cyan", (2, 3): "cyan", (2, 2): "cyan"}, cell_w=1.1)
        if t == 7:
            V.text(ax, p, 0, -0.9,
                   f"last x spent = {p4_raw}; moves = {p4_raw} + 1 = {p4_zans}",
                   size=9, color="green", ha="left")


V.animate(p4_frame, 8, captions=p4_caps, interval=1300)
```

Frames 1–4 cycle surplus forward between three buckets; frames 5–8 read the same residue idea as a schedule over $x = 1, 2, 3, \ldots$

:::

**Reading the animation.** Frames 1–4 are A3's $3$-cycle: the amber cell marks the bucket about to give its excess away, and because a move only ever pushes forward, there is no choice to make — each surplus simply walks one step. Frames 5–8 keep the residue idea but change what is being counted: the cyan cells are the two elements that both need $x \equiv 2 \pmod 3$, and since one value of $x$ can serve only one element, the second of them must wait a full cycle, at $x = 5$. That is why the answer is a max over needs, not a sum: @sec-gcd-p4-balance is the transfer, @sec-gcd-p4-zeromod is the schedule.

{{< include ../problems/cf-1490b-balanced-remainders/problem.qmd >}}

[**From a transfer to a schedule.** 1490B asks how many $+1$ moves balance a residue histogram, and answers with a forward sweep between buckets. 1374D asks how long a counter must climb to *serve* every bucket, and answers with the same histogram read one level up: the busiest need, times the cycle length.]{.flow-bridge}

{{< include ../problems/cf-1374d-zero-remainder-array/problem.qmd >}}

## Pattern 5: Let a Count Replace the Simulation {#sec-gcd-p5}

**When the input is too big to touch.** A6's lesson is that some statements describe a process you could simulate — and then set the numbers so large that simulating is not the intended move. Both problems here are of that shape: the input either never needs to be built at all (a range $[l..r]$ up to $10^9$), or the process looks iterative but collapses into a single left-to-right pass. The common thread is that a **count** — of odd numbers, of how far a factor-run extends — is the whole answer, and the work is in proving which count.

::: {.callout-important title="Template"}
- **Believe the bound, not the verb.** When a statement says "simulate this operation" but sets $r - l$ to $10^9$, the intended answer is a closed-form count, and the operation is decoration (@sec-gcd-a6).
- **Consecutive integers are coprime.** $\gcd(x, x + 1) = 1$ always, so a range of length $\ge 2$ has array gcd $1$ no matter what — the only thing that can differ between ranges is a parity class.
- **One stack pass finds maximal runs.** "Merge adjacent elements that share a factor, repeatedly" is transitive *along a run*: fold each maximal run into its lcm with one left-to-right stack, popping while the top shares a factor (@sec-gcd-a6).
- **Absorb, don't simulate.** When a move pairs two elements into their product, the question is not *which* pair but *how many* elements of the awkward class (odds) exist to be paired — a single count, plus a degenerate case check.
:::

::: {#fig-gcd-anim-p5}

```{python}
#| echo: false
p5_nums = Traces.MR_NUMS                    # [6, 4, 3, 2, 7, 6, 2]
p5_stack, p5_steps = [], []
for p5_x in p5_nums:
    p5_cur, p5_merges = p5_x, 0
    while p5_stack and gcd(p5_stack[-1], p5_cur) > 1:
        p5_top = p5_stack.pop()
        p5_cur = p5_top * p5_cur // gcd(p5_top, p5_cur)
        p5_merges += 1
    p5_stack.append(p5_cur)
    p5_steps.append((p5_x, p5_cur, p5_merges, list(p5_stack)))
assert p5_steps[-1][3] == Traces.MR_ANS == [12, 7, 6]
p5_odds = [(r + 1) // 2 - l // 2 for (l, r, _k) in Traces.PA_TESTS]
assert p5_odds == [1, 2, 1, 0, 3, 3, 1, 4, 3]
p5_caps = [
    "LC 2197: merge adjacent non-coprimes into their lcm, repeatedly, left to right",
    "push 6; push 4: gcd(6, 4) = 2 > 1 -> fold to lcm 12",
    "push 3, then 2: each shares a factor with 12 -> the run keeps folding into 12",
    "push 7: gcd(12, 7) = 1 - the run breaks, 7 stands alone",
    "push 6, then 2: gcd(6, 2) = 2 -> fold to 6; stack is [12, 7, 6], the answer",
    "switch: CF 1629B, a = every integer in [l..r], r - l can be 10^9",
    "two consecutive integers are always coprime, so only the ODD count can matter",
    "odds([l..r]) = (r+1)//2 - l//2; answer is YES iff that count fits in k (or a lone element > 1)",
]


def p5_frame(ax, p, t):
    if t <= 4:
        p5_step_idx = [0, 1, 3, 4, 6][t]
        p5_shown = p5_steps[p5_step_idx]
        V.array(ax, p, p5_nums[:p5_step_idx + 1], colors={p5_step_idx: "amber"},
                label="nums", index=False)
        V.array(ax, p, p5_shown[3], y=-2.2, label="stack", index=False,
                colors={j: "cyan" for j in range(len(p5_shown[3]))})
    else:
        V.grid(ax, p, [["[l..r]", "k", "odds", "verdict"],
                       *[[f"[{l}..{r}]", str(p5_k), str(p5_o), p5_v]
                         for (l, r, p5_k), p5_o, p5_v in zip(Traces.PA_TESTS, p5_odds, Traces.PA_ANS)]],
               colors={(i + 1, 3): ("green" if p5_v == "YES" else "red")
                       for i, p5_v in enumerate(Traces.PA_ANS)}, cell_w=1.1)


V.animate(p5_frame, 8, captions=p5_caps, interval=1300)
```

Frames 1–5 are the stack's first five pushes; frames 6–8 abandon the array entirely for a count over all nine of the statement's cases.

:::

**Reading the animation.** Frames 1–5 are the run-collapsing stack: the amber cursor is the element being pushed, and the cyan row underneath is whatever survives so far — notice $3$ and $2$ never become their own entries, because they fold straight into the $12$ that came before them. Frames 6–8 are a different kind of compression: the whole array $[l..r]$ is replaced by a single number, its odd count, and the amber-free grid is just the statement's own nine cases sorted into two columns. @sec-gcd-p5-merge is the stack; @sec-gcd-p5-parity is the count.

{{< include ../problems/lc-2197-replace-non-coprime-numbers-in-array/problem.qmd >}}

[**From a run to a range.** 2197 still touches every element — a stack walks the array once, folding factor-runs as it goes. 1629B refuses to touch the array at all: $r - l$ can be $10^9$, and the only sensible answer is a closed-form count over the range.]{.flow-bridge}

{{< include ../problems/cf-1629b-gcd-arrays/problem.qmd >}}

**Looking back.** Every pattern in Part B answers the same question — *what am I allowed to throw away?* Pattern 1 keeps two numbers and discards $n - 2$; Pattern 2 keeps a running gcd and cuts at its death; Pattern 3 replaces the $\binom{n}{2}$ pair loop with a $V \ln V$ divisor sweep; Pattern 4 forgets magnitudes entirely and holds a $k$-cell histogram; Pattern 5 abandons the array and keeps one parity count. The chain of coarser and coarser representations is exactly the chain of lessons A1–A6, read backwards: each pattern is one lesson's structural fact promoted to an algorithm.

## Pattern map

| Signal in the statement | Pattern | Section |
|---|---|---|
| "GCD of the smallest and largest element" | Fold endpoints; one gcd call | @sec-gcd-p1-arrgcd |
| "Largest string that tiles both $a$ and $b$" | Fold on lengths: answer is prefix of length $\gcd(|a|,|b|)$ | @sec-gcd-p1-strgcd |
| "Count pairs with equal ratio $w / h$" | Reduce by gcd → canonical key → histogram $\sum \binom{c}{2}$ | @sec-gcd-p2-rects |
| "Split into fewest segments each with gcd $> 1$" | Running gcd; forced cut at death; greedy is provably minimal | @sec-gcd-p2-split |
| "Number of distinct GCDs of all subsequences" | Chain fold $O(n \log V)$, or sieve the value domain | @sec-gcd-p3-subseq |
| "$q$-th smallest pair gcd in sorted list" | Multiple-count sieve → top-down inversion → flatten | @sec-gcd-p3-gcdpair |
| "Balance three residue buckets by $+1$ moves" | Residue histogram; forward-only sweep | @sec-gcd-p4-balance |
| "Zero all elements mod $k$ with a rising counter" | Residue histogram as schedule; $\max_d (\mathit{cnt}[d]-1) \cdot k + d + 1$ | @sec-gcd-p4-zeromod |
| "Merge adjacent non-coprimes into their lcm" | One left-to-right stack pass; fold each factor-run into lcm | @sec-gcd-p5-merge |
| "Can $k$ product-moves make array gcd $> 1$?" ($r - l \le 10^9$) | Pigeonhole: count odds; answer YES iff odds $\le k$ | @sec-gcd-p5-parity |
| "GCD of the array except position $i$" | Prefix/suffix table (no inverse) | @sec-gcd-a1 |
| "Which gcd values are reachable by extending a subarray?" | $O(\log V)$ chain per endpoint | @sec-gcd-a2 |
| "$\varphi(n)$, count of coprimes below $n$" | Sieve Euler's totient; $1 + 2\sum\varphi$ | @sec-gcd-a5 |
| "$n + 1$ integers from $\{1, \dots, 2n\}$ contain a divisor pair" | Pigeonhole on odd parts | @sec-gcd-a6 |

## Pitfalls

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistakes"}
- **Folding all values instead of the two endpoints.** LC 1979 asks for $\gcd(\min, \max)$, not $\gcd$ of the whole array. On `[2, 5, 6, 9, 10]` the two-end fold gives $\gcd(2, 10) = 2$, while folding all five gives $1$ because $2$ divides neither $5$ nor $9$. $[2, 3, 4]$ is the smallest counterexample: $\gcd(2,3,4) = 1$ against $\gcd(2,4) = 2$ (@sec-gcd-p1-arrgcd).
- **Forgetting the $+1$ in CF 1374D.** The last increment for bucket $d$ with $c$ elements is *spent* at $x = (c - 1) \cdot k + d$, but reaching that $x$ costs one more move. On the statement sample `[1, 2, 1, 3]` with $k = 3$: the raw maximum is $5$, the correct answer is $6$, and returning $5$ fails the first sample (@sec-gcd-p4-zeromod).
- **Bucketing by residue instead of by increment.** CF 1374D asks for the increment $d = k - (a_i \bmod k)$, not the residue itself. Two elements with residue $1$ both need $d = 2$, not $d = 1$. The complement is what the counter must hit (@sec-gcd-p4-zeromod, @sec-gcd-a3).
- **Allowing backward surplus transfer in CF 1490B.** An operation is $a_j \mathrel{+}= 1$, which walks an element from bucket $r$ to $(r+1) \bmod 3$; there is no $-1$ operation. Pushing a unit from bucket $0$ to bucket $2$ requires two forward moves ($0 \to 1 \to 2$), so only the *forward* sweep is optimal. A greedy that picks the nearest deficit in either direction is wrong on `[0, 2, 5, 5, 4, 8]` (@sec-gcd-p4-balance).
- **An `int` accumulator in CF 1374D.** With $n \le 2 \cdot 10^5$ and $k \le 10^9$, the formula $(\mathit{cnt}[d] - 1) \cdot k + d$ can reach roughly $2 \cdot 10^{14}$. A 32-bit `int` overflows; use `long long` in C++ and the natural Python `int` (@sec-arr-size-trap).
- **Processing the Möbius inversion bottom-up.** `exact[d]` depends on `exact[m]` for every $m = 2d, 3d, \ldots$, so the outer loop must run $d = V, V-1, \ldots, 1$. A forward sweep reads zeros for the higher multiples and returns `atmost[d]` as `exact[d]` — an overcount that silently inflates small $d$ values (@sec-gcd-a4, @sec-gcd-p3-gcdpair).
- **Merging non-coprimes with gcd instead of lcm.** LC 2197 replaces two adjacent elements that share a factor with their **lcm**. Writing `cur = gcd(top, cur)` collapses `[6, 4, 3, 2]` into $1$ instead of $12$ and destroys the following fold (@sec-gcd-p5-merge).
- **Treating a single-element array as the general case in CF 1629B.** A one-element range `[x..x]` has array gcd $x$, so the answer is YES if $x > 1$ regardless of $k$; the odd-count rule "YES iff odds $\le k$" assumes at least two elements. `[13..13]` with $k = 0$ is YES; `[1..1]` with any $k$ is NO (@sec-gcd-p5-parity, @sec-gcd-a6).
- **Stress-testing the sieve on a full range but not the inversion.** `a4_multiple_counts` and the top-down subtraction can each be wrong without the other triggering a mismatch. Cross-check `sum(exact)` against $\binom{n}{2}$, and compare `exact[1]` against a brute-force count of coprime pairs on random arrays before trusting either (@sec-gcd-a4, @sec-gcd-p3-gcdpair).
- **Re-scanning for the merge stack.** LC 2197's process *looks* like a repeated scan (merge, restart), but a shared factor is transitive along a contiguous run, so one stack pass suffices. The `a6_merge_naive` oracle in @sec-gcd-a6 re-scans and gives the same answer, but the proof that one pass is correct requires checking the transitivity explicitly on small arrays with a fuzz loop (@sec-gcd-p5-merge, @sec-gcd-a6).
- **Believing the gcd chain converges only for large values.** Even a chain of `2, 4, 8, …` (gcd only shrinks to a proper divisor) is bounded by $\lceil \log_2 V \rceil$ steps. With $V = 10^6$ the ceiling is $20$, and the chain length is *at most* that, not approximately — the worst case is Fibonacci-adjacent values, not powers of two (@sec-gcd-a2).
:::

## Exercises

**1. [E] For `[6, 10, 15]`, give `pref`, `suf`, and the "except" gcd at each position. Why is the array gcd 1 even though every pair shares a factor?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
`pref = [6, 2, 1]`, `suf = [1, 5, 15]`, `except = [5, 3, 2]`. The array gcd is $\gcd(6, 10, 15) = 1$, but each *pair* shares a factor: $\gcd(6,10) = 2$, $\gcd(10,15) = 5$, $\gcd(6,15) = 3$. Collective coprimality is strictly weaker than pairwise coprimality — the common factor is different for every pair, so no single integer $> 1$ divides all three (@sec-gcd-a1).
:::

**2. [E] How many Euclid reductions does $\gcd(987, 610)$ take? What about $\gcd(89, 55)$? What is the general bound on the number of steps in terms of $\min(a, b)$?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\gcd(987, 610) = 1$ after $14$ reductions; $\gcd(89, 55) = 1$ after $9$. Both inputs are consecutive Fibonacci numbers ($987 = F(16)$, $610 = F(15)$, $89 = F(11)$, $55 = F(10)$), and Lamé's theorem says the worst case at $\min(a,b)$ is the largest Fibonacci index not exceeding $\min(a,b)$. At $10^9$ the bound is roughly $44$ reductions because $F(45) \approx 1.13 \cdot 10^9$ (@sec-gcd-a1).
:::

**3. [E] List the five rows of `a2_chains([4, 6, 8, 12, 3])` and the maximum row length. Verify $\text{max\_len} \le \lceil \log_2(12) \rceil + 1$.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Rows: `[[4], [2, 6], [2, 8], [2, 4, 12], [1, 3]]`, max length $3$. $\lceil \log_2(12) \rceil + 1 = 4 + 1 = 5$, and $3 \le 5$ ✓. The row at index $3$ is the longest: the four subarrays ending there have gcds $\gcd(12) = 12$, $\gcd(8,12) = 4$, $\gcd(6,8,12) = 2$, $\gcd(4,6,8,12) = 2$, which collapse to $\{2, 4, 12\}$ (@sec-gcd-a2).
:::

**4. [E] CF 1490B: find the residue histogram and the number of moves for `[2, 0, 2, 1, 0, 0]`.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Residues mod $3$: $[2, 0, 2, 1, 0, 0]$, so $\mathit{cnt} = [3, 1, 2]$ and target $= 2$. Bucket $0$ is over by $1$, so one forward move pushes it to bucket $1$: $[2, 2, 2]$. Answer: $1$ move (@sec-gcd-a3, @sec-gcd-p4-balance).
:::

**5. [E] CF 1490B: compute the histogram and moves for `[7, 1, 3, 4, 2, 10, 3, 9, 6]`.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Residues: $7\%3=1$, $1\%3=1$, $3\%3=0$, $4\%3=1$, $2\%3=2$, $10\%3=1$, $3\%3=0$, $9\%3=0$, $6\%3=0$. Histogram $[4, 4, 1]$, target $= 3$. Bucket $0$ has $1$ surplus → push to bucket $1$: $[3, 5, 1]$, $1$ move. Bucket $1$ has $2$ surplus → push both to bucket $2$: $[3, 3, 3]$, $+2$ moves. Total $3$ moves (@sec-gcd-a3).
:::

**6. [M] LC 2001: four rectangles `[(4,8),(3,6),(10,20),(15,30)]` all reduce to key $(1,2)$. Verify $\binom{4}{2} = 6$. Add a fifth rectangle $(3,5)$ and recompute.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\gcd(4,8) = 4$, $\gcd(3,6) = 3$, $\gcd(10,20) = 10$, $\gcd(15,30) = 15$; each reduced form is $(1,2)$. One bucket of size $4$ gives $\binom{4}{2} = 6$ pairs. Adding $(3,5)$: $\gcd(3,5) = 1$, key $(3,5)$. Now two buckets of sizes $4$ and $1$: $\binom{4}{2} + \binom{1}{2} = 6 + 0 = 6$. The new rectangle adds no pair because it does not match any existing key (@sec-gcd-p2-rects, @sec-gcd-a5).
:::

**7. [M] LC 2436: trace the running gcd on `[12, 6, 3, 14, 8]`. Record the segment count at each index, identify the forced cut, and list the segments with their gcds.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Running gcd: $[12, 6, 3, 1, 2]$. Segment count: $[1, 1, 1, 2, 2]$. At index $3$ ($a_3 = 14$): $\gcd(3, 14) = 1$, so a cut is forced and a new segment opens at $14$. Segments: `[12, 6, 3]` (gcd $3$) and `[14, 8]` (gcd $2$). Answer: $2$ (@sec-gcd-p2-split, @sec-gcd-a2).
:::

**8. [M] LC 3312: for `nums = [2, 3, 4]` build $c[d]$ (divisible count), then $\text{atmost}[d] = \binom{c_d}{2}$, then invert top-down to get `exact[d]` for $d = 1, 2, 3, 4$.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$c = [3, 2, 1, 1]$ for $d = 1, 2, 3, 4$. $\text{atmost} = [3, 1, 0, 0]$. Inversion: $\text{exact}[4] = 0$, $\text{exact}[3] = 0$, $\text{exact}[2] = 1 - \text{exact}[4] = 1$, $\text{exact}[1] = 3 - 1 - 0 - 0 = 2$. Check: $\sum \text{exact} = 3 = \binom{3}{2}$ ✓ (@sec-gcd-p3-gcdpair, @sec-gcd-a4).
:::

**9. [M] LC 3312: flatten `exact` from exercise 8 and answer queries $[0, 2, 2]$. Then verify against the brute-force pair gcds.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Flatten: $[1, 1, 2]$ (two $1$s and one $2$). Query $0$: $1$; query $2$: $2$; query $2$: $2$. Brute-force pair gcds: $\gcd(2,3) = 1$, $\gcd(2,4) = 2$, $\gcd(3,4) = 1$, sorted $= [1, 1, 2]$. Answers: $[1, 2, 2]$ ✓ (@sec-gcd-p3-gcdpair).
:::

**10. [M] CF 1374D: for `a = [1, 2, 1, 3]`, $k = 3$, build the `need` dict, compute the raw max, and explain why the answer is raw + 1.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Residues: $[1, 2, 1, 0]$. Elements with nonzero residue need increments $d = 3 - r$: two elements need $d = 2$ (the two $1$s) and one needs $d = 1$ (the $2$). $\mathit{need} = \{2: 2, 1: 1\}$. $\text{raw} = \max((2-1) \cdot 3 + 2,\; (1-1) \cdot 3 + 1) = \max(5, 1) = 5$. The move that spends $x = 5$ is the *sixth* counter tick (moves $0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5$), so the answer is $5 + 1 = 6$ (@sec-gcd-p4-zeromod, @sec-gcd-a3).
:::

**11. [M] CF 1629B: compute `a6_odds` for `[4..10]`, `[1..7]`, and `[3..7]`. For each range and the given $k$, state the verdict.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\mathit{odds}(4,10) = 11//2 - 4//2 = 5 - 2 = 3$ (odds: $5, 7, 9$). $\mathit{odds}(1,7) = 8//2 - 1//2 = 4 - 0 = 4$ (odds: $1, 3, 5, 7$). $\mathit{odds}(3,7) = 8//2 - 3//2 = 4 - 1 = 3$ (odds: $3, 5, 7$). Verdicts: `[4..10]` with $k=3$: $3 \le 3$ → YES. `[1..7]` with $k=3$: $4 > 3$ → NO. `[3..7]` with $k=4$: $3 \le 4$ → YES (@sec-gcd-p5-parity, @sec-gcd-a6).
:::

**12. [M] LC 2197: trace the stack on `[4, 6, 8, 3]` step by step. Then on `[2, 2, 1, 1, 3, 3, 3]`.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
`[4, 6, 8, 3]`: push $4$; push $6$, $\gcd(4,6) = 2 > 1$ → pop, $\text{lcm} = 12$; push $8$, $\gcd(12,8) = 4 > 1$ → pop, $\text{lcm} = 24$; push $3$, $\gcd(24,3) = 3 > 1$ → pop, $\text{lcm} = 24$. Stack: `[24]`.
`[2, 2, 1, 1, 3, 3, 3]`: push $2$; push $2$, $\gcd(2,2) = 2$ → pop, $\text{lcm} = 2$; push $1$, $\gcd(2,1) = 1$ → stop; push $1$; push $3$, $\gcd(1,3) = 1$ → stop; push $3$; push $3$, $\gcd(3,3) = 3$ → pop, $\text{lcm} = 3$. Stack: `[2, 1, 1, 3]` (@sec-gcd-p5-merge, @sec-gcd-a6).
:::

**13. [H] Verify the chain bound on `[6, 12, 3, 18, 9, 27]` (values up to $V = 27$). List every row of `a2_chains`, the maximum row length, and $\lceil \log_2 27 \rceil$.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Rows: `[[6], [6, 12], [3], [3, 18], [3, 9], [3, 9, 27]]`, max length $3$. $\lceil \log_2 27 \rceil = 5$, and $3 \le 5$ ✓. The row at index $5$ is longest: the six subarrays ending at $27$ have gcds $27, 9, 9, 9, 9, 3$ which collapse to $\{3, 9, 27\}$. The bound is $\lceil \log_2 V \rceil$ because each strict drop in the chain goes to a proper divisor, which is at most half (@sec-gcd-a2).
:::

**14. [H] Enumerate all non-empty subsequences of `[6, 10, 3]`, compute each gcd, and verify the result matches `a2_all_gcds` (the union of all chain rows).**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Singles: $\gcd(6)=6$, $\gcd(10)=10$, $\gcd(3)=3$. Pairs: $\gcd(6,10)=2$, $\gcd(6,3)=3$, $\gcd(10,3)=1$. Triple: $\gcd(6,10,3)=1$. Union: $\{1, 2, 3, 6, 10\}$, five values. Chain rows: `[[6], [2, 10], [1, 3]]`; union of rows $= \{1, 2, 3, 6, 10\}$ ✓ (@sec-gcd-a2, @sec-gcd-p3-subseq).
:::

**15. [H] CF 1629B: run `a6_min_moves_bfs` on `[3..5]` and confirm that the BFS minimum equals the odd count. Explain why $[3..5]$ with $k = 1$ is NO but with $k = 2$ is YES.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$[3, 4, 5]$ has $\mathit{odds} = 2$ (the elements $3$ and $5$). BFS: start gcd $= 1$; after one product-merge we still have two elements with gcd $1$ (e.g. $[15, 4]$: $\gcd = 1$); after two merges all three are one element $= 60$, gcd $= 60 > 1$. So `a6_min_moves_bfs(3, 5) = 2 = odds`. With $k = 1$: need $2 \le 1$ fails → NO. With $k = 2$: need $2 \le 2$ holds → YES (@sec-gcd-p5-parity, @sec-gcd-a6).
:::

## Interview questions

**1. Why does Euclid's algorithm run in $O(\log \min(a, b))$ steps, and what inputs produce the worst case?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Each step replaces $(a, b)$ with $(b, a \bmod b)$, and after two steps the larger entry has at least halved, because $a \bmod b < b$ and the chain of remainders is strictly decreasing. Consecutive Fibonacci numbers are the worst case: $\gcd(F(n{+}1), F(n))$ takes exactly $n - 1$ reductions. At $10^9$ the largest Fibonacci not exceeding it is $F(44)$, so the bound is around $44$ reductions (@sec-gcd-a1).
:::

**2. How do you compute "the gcd of the array except position $i$" in $O(n)$?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Build `pref[i]` left to right and `suf[i]` right to left. Then the answer is $\gcd(\mathit{pref}[i-1],\; \mathit{suf}[i+1])$, with $\gcd(0, x) = x$ handling the boundary cases. The key is that gcd is associative but has **no inverse**, so you cannot subtract the contribution of position $i$ from a single fold — you need a second table (@sec-gcd-a1).
:::

**3. Why is the gcd of all subarrays ending at position $i$ at most $\lceil \log_2 V \rceil$ distinct values, and what algorithm does that enable?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Each strict drop in the gcd chain lands on a proper divisor, which is at most half. Starting at $V$, at most $\lceil \log_2 V \rceil$ halvings reach $1$. So you can fold the gcd set over positions in $O(n \log V)$ total, rather than enumerating $\binom{n+1}{2}$ subarrays. This is the technique behind LC 1819 and the $O(n \log V)$ complexity class of all "distinct subarray gcd" problems (@sec-gcd-a2).
:::

**4. Given an array of rectangles $(w_i, h_i)$, how do you count pairs with $w_i / h_i = w_j / h_j$ without floating point?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Reduce each pair by its gcd: $\mathit{key}(w, h) = (w / g,\; h / g)$. Two ratios are equal exactly when their reduced forms are identical, so you build a histogram of canonical keys and compute $\sum_{\mathit{key}} \binom{c}{2}$. On `[(4,8),(3,6),(10,20),(15,30)]` all four reduce to $(1,2)$, giving $\binom{4}{2} = 6$ (@sec-gcd-p2-rects, @sec-gcd-a5).
:::

**5. Explain the greedy for splitting an array into the fewest contiguous segments with gcd $> 1$, and why it is provably minimal.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Maintain a running gcd $g$; extend the current segment while $\gcd(g, a_i) > 1$; the instant $\gcd(g, a_i) = 1$, cut and restart at $a_i$. The proof is that gcd only shrinks — once it reaches $1$ no future element can raise it, so any segment containing that pair is doomed. The cut is *forced*, and the greedy is minimal by exchange: any valid partition must have at least as many segments as the greedy creates (@sec-gcd-p2-split, @sec-gcd-a2).
:::

**6. How do you count how many elements in an array are divisible by each $d \le V$, and what is the total work?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Build a frequency table `freq[v]`, then for each $d = 1, 2, \ldots, V$, sum `freq[m]` over multiples $m = d, 2d, 3d, \ldots \le V$. Total reads: $\sum_{d \le V} V / d \approx V \ln V$. At $V = 10^5$ this is $1{,}166{,}750$; at $V = 10^6$ it is $13{,}970{,}034$. The cost is independent of $n$ (@sec-gcd-a4).
:::

**7. How do you go from "$\binom{c_d}{2}$ pairs have gcd a multiple of $d$" to "$\mathit{exact}[d]$ pairs have gcd exactly $d$"?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Process $d$ from $V$ down to $1$. Initialize $\mathit{exact}[d] = \binom{c_d}{2}$, then subtract $\mathit{exact}[m]$ for every multiple $m = 2d, 3d, \ldots$. The top-down order ensures all higher multiples are already finalized. The total inversion cost is the same $V \ln V$ harmonic sum. This is the Möbius principle in its simplest form (@sec-gcd-a4).
:::

**8. What is the $3$-cycle balance problem (CF 1490B), and why does only a forward sweep work?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
You have $n$ integers, $3 \mid n$, and an operation adds $1$ to one element. Adding $1$ walks it from bucket $r$ to $(r+1) \bmod 3$; there is no backward move. So surplus can only flow in one direction around the cycle. The optimal plan is a single forward sweep: for each bucket, hand its excess to the next bucket. The answer for `[0, 2, 5, 5, 4, 8]` is $3$ moves (@sec-gcd-p4-balance, @sec-gcd-a3).
:::

**9. In CF 1374D, why is the answer $\max_d (\mathit{cnt}[d]-1) \cdot k + d + 1$ and not a sum?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Each move picks one element and adds the current counter value $x$ to it, then $x$ advances. Elements in bucket $d$ are served at $x = d, d + k, d + 2k, \ldots$, and each $x$ serves exactly one element. So the *last* move happens at $x = (\mathit{cnt}[d]-1) \cdot k + d$ for whichever bucket has the highest such $x$ (the $\max$), and reaching that $x$ takes one more increment (the $+1$). Summing would double-count: the counter is shared across all buckets (@sec-gcd-p4-zeromod, @sec-gcd-a3).
:::

**10. In LC 2197, why is one stack pass sufficient to simulate the repeated-merge process?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
A shared factor is *transitive along a contiguous run*: if $\gcd(a_i, a_{i+1}) > 1$ and $\gcd(a_{i+1}, a_{i+2}) > 1$, the entire run folds into one lcm. A stack processes left to right, popping and folding whenever the top shares a factor with the new element. This is equivalent to merging all pairs and re-scanning, because the fold is associative ($\text{lcm}(\text{lcm}(a,b),c) = \text{lcm}(a,\text{lcm}(b,c))$). `[6, 4, 3, 2, 7, 6, 2]` gives `[12, 7, 6]` in one pass (@sec-gcd-p5-merge, @sec-gcd-a6).
:::

**11. CF 1629B: how do you decide the answer without touching the array?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$\gcd(x, x+1) = 1$ always, so any range $[l..r]$ with $r - l \ge 1$ has array gcd $1$. A product-move absorbs one odd element (pairing it with an even). The odd count in $[l..r]$ is $(r+1)//2 - l//2$. The answer is YES iff that count $\le k$. One-element ranges are exceptions: $[x..x]$ has gcd $x$, so $[13..13]$ with $k=0$ is YES. At $r - l = 10^9$ this is the only feasible approach (@sec-gcd-p5-parity, @sec-gcd-a6).
:::

**12. What is Euler's totient function, and how does it count coprime pairs in $[1..n]^2$?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$\varphi(k)$ counts $1 \le j \le k$ with $\gcd(j, k) = 1$, computed as $k \prod_{p \mid k} (1 - 1/p)$ from prime factors. In the grid $[1..n]^2$, the diagonal $i = j$ is coprime only at $(1,1)$, and the upper triangle contributes $\sum_{k=2}^n \varphi(k)$ while the lower triangle mirrors it. Total: $1 + 2\sum_{k=2}^n \varphi(k)$. At $n = 5$: $1 + 2(1+2+2+4) = 19$ (@sec-gcd-a5).
:::

**13. You need to answer "how many elements are divisible by $d$?" for every $d \le V$. Give three rungs of a ladder and the crossover.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Rung 1: for each query $d$, scan all $n$ elements — $O(n)$ per query. Rung 2: for each $d$, walk multiples in a frequency table — $O(V \ln V)$ precompute, $O(1)$ per query. Rung 3: if queries arrive online with varying $d$ and updates change the array, use a Fenwick tree over multiples or a divisor lattice. The crossover is when the number of queries $Q$ satisfies $Q \cdot n > V \ln V$: at $V = 10^5$ that's $Q > n / 12$ roughly. The harmonic sieve (rung 2) is always the right answer for offline batches when $V \le 10^6$ (@sec-gcd-a4).
:::

**14. What is the pigeonhole argument that $n + 1$ integers from $\{1, \dots, 2n\}$ always contain a divisor pair?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Write each integer as $x = 2^a \cdot o$ (odd part $o$). In $[1..2n]$ there are exactly $n$ distinct odd parts ($1, 3, 5, \ldots, 2n-1$). By the pigeonhole principle, choosing $n + 1$ integers forces two to share the same odd part $o$. Those two are $2^a \cdot o$ and $2^b \cdot o$ with (WLOG) $a < b$, so the first divides the second. The proof is the bucket structure of odd parts, not any search (@sec-gcd-a6).
:::

**15. A statement says $n \le 2 \cdot 10^5$, $a_i \le 10^5$, and asks a question about divisibility of pairs. What is your first move?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Check whether the value bound ($10^5$) is small enough to own a table. $\sum_{d \le V} V/d = 1.17 \cdot 10^6$ steps precompute the multiple counts $c[d]$ for every divisor simultaneously. Then $\binom{c_d}{2}$ gives the "at most" count, and the top-down inversion gives "exactly $d$" in the same harmonic total. The pair loop is $\binom{2 \cdot 10^5}{2} \approx 2 \cdot 10^{10}$, which is clearly too slow; the sieve is $\sim 10^6$, which is comfortable. This is Pattern 3 (@sec-gcd-p3, @sec-gcd-a4).
:::

**16. How do you stress-test the harmonic sieve and the top-down inversion?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Three checks. (1) `sum(exact[d] for d in 1..V)` must equal $\binom{n}{2}$ — every pair has some gcd. (2) Fuzz over small arrays (values $\le 25$, $n \le 7$) comparing `exact[d]` against a brute-force Counter of all pair gcds, for $\sim 60$ random cases. (3) Invert the test: compute $\sum_{m: d \mid m} \mathit{exact}[m]$ and check it equals $\binom{c_d}{2}$ — the original at-most count. The inversion is the most error-prone step, and a wrong loop order (bottom-up) passes test (1) but fails test (2) informatively (@sec-gcd-a4).
:::

## Summary

::: {.callout-important title="Templates to remember"}
- **The fold and its two tables.** `g = 0; for x in a: g = gcd(g, x)` answers the gcd of the whole array. "Except position $i$" needs `pref` and `suf` because gcd has no inverse (@sec-gcd-a1).
- **The chain lemma.** Distinct gcds of subarrays ending at position $i$ form a chain of proper divisors: length $\le \lceil \log_2 V \rceil + 1$. Fold the set, not the windows (@sec-gcd-a2).
- **Residue histogram.** When only $a_i \bmod k$ matters, replace the array by $k$ counters; a $+1$ move is a bucket transfer; a rising counter is a schedule (@sec-gcd-a3, @sec-gcd-p4).
- **Harmonic sieve.** Iterate divisors, not pairs: $\sum_{d \le V} V / d \approx V \ln V$. Invert "multiple of $d$" to "exactly $d$" top-down (@sec-gcd-a4).
- **Coprime pairs and canonical keys.** $\varphi$ counts coprimes to $k$ below $k$; reducing a ratio by its gcd turns equality into a histogram bucket (@sec-gcd-a5).
- **Pigeonhole counts.** $\gcd(x, x+1) = 1$; odd parts in $[1..2n]$ are $n$ buckets; the odd count in $[l..r]$ is $(r+1)//2 - l//2$. When the input is too large to touch, one count is the answer (@sec-gcd-a6).
:::

- The entire chapter lives in the tension between two loops: one over **positions** ($n$, with a fold) and one over **values or divisors** ($V$, with a sieve). The skill is recognizing from the constraint line which loop is cheap and which is hopeless, and then finding the right invariant to carry through it (@sec-gcd-why).
- GCD is associative but has no inverse, so the one-pass running sum trick does not transfer. The repair is a second table read from the right, and the identity element is $\gcd(0, x) = x$ — the same seed discipline as `cnt[0] = 1` in @sec-cnt-a4 (@sec-gcd-a1).
- The chain of distinct gcds is short ($O(\log V)$ per endpoint) because every strict shrink goes to a proper divisor, which is at most half. This is what makes "all subarrays" gcd problems tractable at $n = 10^5$, and it also makes the greedy split provably optimal: once the fold dies, it stays dead (@sec-gcd-a2, @sec-gcd-p2-split).
- The residue histogram is @sec-cnt-a3's frequency table with the bucket index chosen by a modulus instead of a value. What makes this chapter different is that the *operations* in the statements are themselves moves between buckets — a $+1$ is a step on the $3$-cycle, a rising counter is a schedule — so the question reduces to arithmetic on the counters alone (@sec-gcd-a3, @sec-gcd-p4).
- The harmonic sieve ($\sum_d V/d$) is the workhorse for any batch of divisor questions. The top-down inversion from "at-least" to "exactly" is the Möbius principle at its simplest, and the order of the loop is the single most common bug: process $d = V, V-1, \ldots, 1$, never the reverse (@sec-gcd-a4).
- Pigeonhole and parity arguments replace simulation when constraints make touching the array impossible. Two consecutive integers are coprime, odd parts are only $n$ in $[1..2n]$, and the odd count in a range decides CF 1629B — all one-line facts that take more work to *find* than to *verify* (@sec-gcd-a6).

Ordered by pattern, following the five-part climb. The ten problems solved in Part B are marked `.solved`; every other entry is "solve it after the lesson named."

::: {.practice}
- [LC 1979 · Find Greatest Common Divisor of Array](https://leetcode.com/problems/find-greatest-common-divisor-of-array/){.solved difficulty="Easy"} — fold the two endpoints, not all $n$ values (@sec-gcd-p1-arrgcd).
- [LC 1071 · Greatest Common Divisor of Strings](https://leetcode.com/problems/greatest-common-divisor-of-strings/){.solved difficulty="Easy"} — the operator travels: fold on string lengths, verify with a concatenation test (@sec-gcd-p1-strgcd).
- [LC 2001 · Number of Pairs of Interchangeable Rectangles](https://leetcode.com/problems/number-of-pairs-of-interchangeable-rectangles/){.solved difficulty="Medium"} — reduce by gcd, histogram, $\sum \binom{c}{2}$ (@sec-gcd-p2-rects).
- [LC 2436 · Minimum Split Into Subarrays With GCD Greater Than One](https://leetcode.com/problems/minimum-split-into-subarrays-with-gcd-greater-than-one/){.solved difficulty="Medium"} — running gcd as a forced-cut greedy (@sec-gcd-p2-split).
- [LC 1819 · Number of Different Subsequences GCDs](https://leetcode.com/problems/number-of-different-subsequences-gcds/){.solved difficulty="Hard"} — the value-domain sieve: test "gcd of all multiples of $d$ equals $d$" (@sec-gcd-p3-subseq).
- [LC 3312 · Sorted GCD Pair Queries](https://leetcode.com/problems/sorted-gcd-pair-queries/){.solved difficulty="Hard"} — multiple counts, top-down inversion, answer order statistics without building the pair list (@sec-gcd-p3-gcdpair).
- [CF 1490B · Balanced Remainders](https://codeforces.com/problemset/problem/1490/B){.solved rating="1000"} — residue histogram with forward-only surplus transfer (@sec-gcd-p4-balance).
- [CF 1374D · Zero Remainder Array](https://codeforces.com/problemset/problem/1374/D){.solved rating="1400"} — residue histogram as a schedule; the $+1$ and the bucket-by-increment traps (@sec-gcd-p4-zeromod).
- [LC 2197 · Replace Non-Coprime Numbers in Array](https://leetcode.com/problems/replace-non-coprime-numbers-in-array/){.solved difficulty="Hard"} — one stack pass folding factor-runs by lcm (@sec-gcd-p5-merge).
- [CF 1629B · GCD Arrays](https://codeforces.com/problemset/problem/1629/B){.solved rating="800"} — pigeonhole: the odd count decides (@sec-gcd-p5-parity).
- [CF 1490F · Equalize the Array](https://codeforces.com/problemset/problem/1490/F){rating="1500"} — frequency-of-frequency histogram with a small value domain; the same bucket-transfer structure as 1490B in a different costume (@sec-gcd-a3, @sec-gcd-a4).
- [LC 974 · Subarray Sums Divisible by K](https://leetcode.com/problems/subarray-sums-divisible-by-k/){difficulty="Medium"} — prefix residue histogram with a complementary lookup; @sec-cnt-a4's sweep mod $k$ (@sec-gcd-a3).
- [LC 1509 · Replace All ?s to Balance a String](https://leetcode.com/problems/replace-all-s-to-balance-a-string/){difficulty="Medium"} — greedy with residue-style targets; the forward-only transfer as an intuition pump (@sec-gcd-a3).
- [LC 2163 · Minimum Difference in Sums After Removal of Elements](https://leetcode.com/problems/minimum-difference-in-sums-after-removal-of-elements/){difficulty="Hard"} — prefix/suffix fold structure (here max-heap instead of gcd), the same two-table shape as @sec-gcd-a1.
- [CSES 2207 · Euler Set](https://cses.fi/problemset/task/2207){rating="advanced"} — compute $\varphi$ for many values via a sieve; directly applies @sec-gcd-a5's totient machinery.
- [LC 1201 · Ugly Number III](https://leetcode.com/problems/ugly-number-iii/){difficulty="Medium"} — inclusion–exclusion over divisors; harmonic-style counting over a value domain (@sec-gcd-a4).
- [CF 1034A · Enlarge GCD](https://codeforces.com/problemset/problem/1034/A){rating="1800"} — remove the fewest elements so gcd of the rest is $> 1$; the sieve and $\varphi$ machinery of @sec-gcd-a4 and @sec-gcd-a5 applied to a deletion problem.
- [LC 1395 · Count Number of Teams](https://leetcode.com/problems/count-number-of-teams/){difficulty="Medium"} — fix the middle, multiply (see @sec-cnt-p4-teams): contrast with gcd's non-multiplicative structure (@sec-gcd-a2).
- [SPOJ GCDEX — GCD Extreme](https://www.spoj.com/problems/GCDEX/){difficulty="advanced"} — sum $\gcd(i,j)$ over all pairs $i < j \le n$: combine the harmonic sieve with the Möbius inversion of @sec-gcd-a4.
:::

## Further reading

- [CP-Algorithms — Euclidean Algorithm](https://cp-algorithms.com/algebra/euclid-algorithm.html) — proof of Lamé's theorem, the Fibonacci worst case, and the binary gcd variant.
- [CP-Algorithms — Sieve of Eratosthenes](https://cp-algorithms.com/algebra/sieve-of-eratosthenes.html) — the $O(V \log \log V)$ prime sieve and the linear sieve, both used in @sec-gcd-a4's multiple counts.
- [CP-Algorithms — Euler Totient Function](https://cp-algorithms.com/algebra/phi-function.html) — the product formula $\varphi(n) = n \prod_{p|n}(1 - 1/p)$, the sieve that computes all $\varphi$ up to $V$, and the sum-of-coprimes identity used in @sec-gcd-a5.
- [Wikipedia — Greatest Common Divisor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greatest_common_divisor) — algebraic properties (associativity, the absence of an inverse, $\gcd \cdot \mathrm{lcm} = ab$) and the gcd of multiple integers via pairwise fold.
- [Wikipedia — Pigeonhole Principle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pigeonhole_principle) — the odd-parts argument of @sec-gcd-a6 and its classical application to divisor pairs in $\{1, \dots, 2n\}$.
- [CP-Algorithms — Inclusion-Exclusion Principle](https://cp-algorithms.com/combinatorics/inclusion-exclusion.html) — the general Möbius-style inversion behind the "at-least to exactly" subtraction of @sec-gcd-a4, with contest applications on pair-gcd sums.
- [CSES 1713 · Counting Divisors](https://cses.fi/problemset/task/1713) and [CSES 1083 · Prime Multiples](https://cses.fi/problemset/task/1083) — direct exercises on the value-domain sieve of @sec-gcd-a4; [CSES 2207 · Euler Set](https://cses.fi/problemset/task/2207) applies @sec-gcd-a5's totient machinery.
- [Competitive Programmer's Handbook (Laaksonen), Ch. 23 — Number Theory](https://cses.fi/book/book.pdf) — a compact contest-oriented treatment of gcd, lcm, modular arithmetic, the sieve, and Euler's theorem, aligned with this chapter's coverage.
